lectures.title: Installing Packages for Local (On-Device) Data Storage

cues.en: So now to conclude this section,
I wanna make sure that the data is stored on the device
and therefore not lost if the app is restarted.
Now I wanna do this from inside my provider here
from inside the UserPlacesNotifier class to be precise.
Here we're adding a new place,
and it's here where I then also wanna store my place data
on the disc of this device.
And when it comes to storing the data,
that means that I wanna store the title
and also the location data, the coordinates,
and the human readable address.
But I also wanna store the image
because at the moment I'm using the image,
which is returned by image picker.
And this image picker image that we're getting back,
this picked image is actually stored
in a temporary location.
So it might be deleted from that location
by the mobile phone without us doing anything.
So we can't rely on the image to stay there.
It might be deleted by the operating system
to free up some space.
So, we should actually move that image
to a more persistent location.
And I wanna do that as part of this addPlace method
in this provider class,
in this notifier class to be precise as well.
Now, to store the data on the local device,
we'll need to install a couple of packages,
for example, Flutter path provider,
which is a package that will give us easy access
to the path where we should store the image,
so that it's not going to be deleted
by the operating system.
This package gives us easy access to a path
that we may use to store data
that belongs to our application.
So we will need to install this package here
by running Flutter pub add path provider,
which is what I'm doing here.
And once this is installed,
we'll also need to install the Flutter path package,
which might sound similar,
but is a different package
that simply simplifies the process
of working with file paths
because we'll need to construct some paths manually
and this package simply makes it easier to construct paths,
such that they work on different operating systems.
For that, we should also install this package here
by using Flutter pub add,
actually this second command here.
So here, I'll run Flutter pub add path.
And last but not least, with that installed,
I also want to install the sqflite package,
Flutter sqflite.
And that is a package that will allow us
to store data on the device using SQL commands.
It essentially helps us create a basic SQL database
on the device and store data, like the title of a place
or the location coordinates in that database.
So that's now not a database running on some server,
but a database that runs locally on the device
where our app runs.
Now I will say that using SQL lite
for storing data on the device is just one option.
You could, for example,
also use the shared preferences package.
This is another package that allows you
to store data on the device,
though it's a bit more basic than the sqflite package.
With shared preferences, you store simple key value pairs.
With sqflite, you have that full database which you can use,
which is why I am using this package here.
So we'll also install this here in our Flutter project
by running this command.
Now with all these packages installed, we can get started.

cues.en: So now to finish this map screen,
I now wanna make sure
that we can also tap on this map to select a new place.
Now for that, we need to listen for taps on the map,
and thankfully that's straightforward,
because the Google Map widget has a on tap parameter,
which can be set to a function
that automatically receives the position
on which the user tapped.
And that position will be such a lat longitude object.
Now here on the map, I then actually wanna move the marker
to that position on which the user tapped.
And I of course also wanna make sure
that if that save button here in the app bar is tapped,
so when this function here is triggered,
that this picked location is sent back
to that add place screen.
Now therefore, I'll first of all add a new variable here
of type lat longitude, which might be null,
which will be my picked location.
And I wanna update this when the map is tapped.
So here on tap, I'll call set state
to also trigger the build method again,
and set picked location equal
to that position I'm getting here.
Now with that we can also move the marker
by going down to that marker.
And here the position should not always be set
to the widget location latitude and longitude.
Instead, I want to check if picked location is not null.
And if that's the case, I want to set my latitude
and longitude to the picked location.
So therefore, here, I'll check if that is not equal to null,
in which case I want to set picked location here
as a value here for position.
Otherwise, I'll use this manually
constructed latitude/longitude value.
Now picked location here could be null.
Dart does not understand that here I'm checking
for it to not be null.
Hence we must add an exclamation mark.
And with that, we implemented this check,
and we have these two alternatives now.
By the way,
you could also write this
in a more concise way by using this syntax,
these double question marks.
This special Dart operator simply says that you want
to use this value here as a value
for this parameter if it's not null,
but if it should be null.
So if picked location should be null here,
you want to use this as a fallback instead.
So that's simply a more concise
and shorter way of getting the same result.
But with that, we're moving the marker,
and I actually don't even want
to show a marker if we don't have a picked location.
So therefore here for markers, we can check
